name: Belladonna eye drops

lead: Belladonna eye drops were made from the deadly nightshade plant and used, especially by women in Renaissance Italy, to dilate the pupils. Larger pupils were considered attractive, and the plant's common name means 'beautiful woman' in Italian.

The effect comes from atropine and related alkaloids, which block receptors that constrict the pupil. The same compounds are among the most toxic found in plants, which is why the practice is documented mainly as history.

paras: Historically, drops from the plant were placed in the eyes to widen the pupils for social occasions. Modern pharmacy uses purified atropine for eye examinations under medical supervision; this article does not describe preparation.

Reported effects include blurred and distorted vision, difficulty focusing on near objects, light sensitivity and faster heart rate; prolonged use was reputed to cause blindness. Systemic poisoning can cause confusion, hallucinations and convulsions.

angle.text: Atropine-type alkaloids widen the pupil, which makes the iris look smaller and the eyes darker. Historically this was the goal of the cosmetic use.

lead: Belladonna eye drops are a historic cosmetic practice: extracts of Atropa belladonna were used to dilate the pupils, an effect long regarded as attractive.[1]

The species name and common name reflect this: bella donna is Italian for 'beautiful woman', and Linnaeus referenced the Renaissance cosmetic use when naming the plant.[1] The drops act as muscarinic antagonists, blocking receptors in the eye muscles that constrict the pupil; the main active compound is atropine, alongside scopolamine and hyoscyamine.[1]
The plant is described as among the most toxic known, and cosmetic-style exposure can cause visual distortions and difficulty focusing up close.[1] The practice is now rarely used cosmetically.[1]

paras: The name belladonna is traced to the plant's historic use by women, since the Italian phrase means beautiful woman; drops from it were widely claimed to dilate women's pupils.[1] Atropine was purified from belladonna in the 1830s and has accepted medical uses.[1]
Belladonna's alkaloids are anticholinergic: they block muscarinic receptors in the muscles of the eye that constrict the pupil, so the pupil widens.[1]

The plant is among the most toxic known. Effects include minor visual distortion, trouble focusing on near objects and a faster pulse; poisoning can add light sensitivity, blurred vision, confusion, hallucinations and convulsions.[1] Prolonged use was reputed to cause blindness.[1] Physostigmine or pilocarpine is the antidote, as for atropine.[1]

timeline.event: Belladonna drops used cosmetically to dilate pupils.[1]
